analysis.one_liner: Requires the IRS to offer free online tax preparation and filing software to all taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing, vote, or any action beyond referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the IRS to build and run free online tax preparation and filing software, let taxpayers download the wage and income records already reported to the IRS, and let people with simple finances have the IRS pre-fill their return for review. It also barred the IRS from signing any agreement with outside companies that would limit its right to offer its own filing services. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of taxpayers, especially people with simple finances who now pay for commercial software or a preparer, would get free filing directly from the IRS and would not have to re-enter data the government already has.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the IRS to establish free online tax preparation and filing software by January 2019, with no fee for any participant [S3].

Requires the IRS to let taxpayers download the wage, interest, and dividend information already reported by employers and banks, delivered within 15 days of receipt in a form that works with tax software [S3].

Creates a voluntary program letting people with simple situations—wages, interest, or dividends only, taking the standard deduction—have the IRS prepare their return, which they then review and submit [S3].

Bars the Treasury Secretary from entering any agreement that restricts the government's right to provide tax preparation or filing services, and speeds up employer and bank reporting deadlines so the data is available before filing season [S3].
Requires the IRS to help states that want to offer similar free filing, including sharing federal return data for state returns [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation and software companies would lose customers and revenue, and the IRS would need congressional funding to build and run the programs.

drawbacks.text: Building and running free IRS filing software requires new funding and technical capacity; the bill authorizes appropriations for fiscal years 2018 through 2022 but provides no dedicated revenue [S3].

The IRS-prepared-return program starts narrow: for 2018 it covers only unmarried filers with no dependents, no self-employment income, and only wages, interest, or dividends, so most filers would initially still need other options [S3].

Tax preparation companies argue that government-prepared returns create a conflict of interest, since the same agency collecting the tax would prepare the return, and that private competition drives innovation—points a good-faith skeptic would raise even though taxpayers bear no fee under this bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For taxpayers with simple returns, the benefits are concrete: free filing and no re-typing data the IRS already has. The main costs fall on tax preparation companies, not on taxpayers directly, though building the system requires real IRS funding. The initial eligibility limits mean the biggest savings would reach the simplest returns first, but the bill lets the IRS expand eligibility over time.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on July 27, 2017, joined by seven Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
Eight Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no further step of any kind after the referral [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and bills that never leave committee die at the end of a Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Paid tax preparation and software companies keep their customer base and revenue; taxpayers keep paying to file.

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require free IRS tax preparation and filing.

for.name: Eight Democratic representatives
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Suozzi, Raskin, Napolitano, Norton, Beyer, and Ryan of Ohio.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Kevin Brady (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee after referral.

against.name: Tax preparation software industry
against.role: Companies selling paid filing software, such as Intuit and H&R Block
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed government-run free filing, which would compete directly with its paid products, and has worked to keep the IRS out of return preparation.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were Democrats; the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: Free IRS filing software and IRS-prepared returns would compete directly with paid products like TurboTax, cutting the industry's core revenue from simple returns. The bill's bar on agreements restricting IRS filing services targeted the arrangement under which the industry runs the existing 'Free File' program.
A free government option for simple returns would draw away customers, particularly lower-income and straightforward filers who now pay for preparation.
